## Key finding

The first implementation indexed `StringView` with `get_char(pos)` while using `char_length()` as the length. Those APIs disagree: `get_char` is UTF-16-code-unit indexed but `char_length` counts code points, so astral characters (e.g. emoji) made the parser either raise "unterminated quoted field" or loop allocating until the wasm heap trapped (the public round-trip property test failed). The parser now decodes the input once via `StringView::to_array()` and walks an `Array[Char]` by code-point index, which round-trips astral content exactly.

## Key design points

- **Continuation decided on the raw line before any decoding** — an odd-length trailing backslash run joins the next physical line, an even run is escaped literals (so `\\` stays a literal and `\`'s marker is never confused with it). Blank/comment lines and quote-opening lines never continue, so a quote left open at end of line is rejected rather than swallowed.
- **Section names** = trimmed inner text; brackets inside are rejected (nesting), and one wrapping quote pair is stripped — so `[remote "origin"]` keeps its quotes while `["quoted section"]` loses them.
- **Values**: leading quote selects the carrier; unquoted strips an inline `;`/`#` only when preceded by whitespace, then trims; each carrier decodes its own escape set and leaves everything else (backslash included) verbatim.
- **`print` always uses the double-quoted carrier** for values and quotes every section name, escaping exactly the decoded set — so `parse(print(doc)) == doc` holds generally, not just for fixtures.
- Empty sections are registered at header time, so they round-trip.

I've implemented the streaming Protocol Buffers wire-format codec. Here's the summary.

## What was built

A genuine, schema-less Protobuf wire-format codec in MoonBit, layered from bytes upward:

| File | Responsibility |
|------|----------------|
| `errors.mbt` | `DecodeError` suberror: `Truncated` / `Malformed(String)` |
| `readers.mbt` | `BytesReader`, `LimitedReader`, and read-exactly / skip-exactly / chunked-payload plumbing |
| `varint.mbt` | varint read/write (10-byte limit, overflow/truncation) and ZigZag32/64 |
| `decode.mbt` | typed readers, keys, length-delimited records, packed fields, unknown-field/group skipping |
| `encode.mbt` | typed writers for all scalars, canonical minimal encoding |

The opaque types `BytesReader` and `LimitedReader[T]` have private fields, so they remain constructible only in-package (`moon info` emits `// private fields`). `moon.pkg` gained the `moonbitlang/core/encoding/utf8` import.

## Key implementation points

- **Streaming**: every decoder loops over `Reader::read`, which may return short. `read_varint64`, `read_exact_into` (4/8-byte values), `read_exact_bytes`, and `skip_exact` all gather across as many calls as needed and raise `Truncated` at end of stream.
- **`LimitedReader`**: uses MoonBit's aliasing of structs with mutable fields so `read_packed` can pass the window by value to the element decoder repeatedly while sharing the `remaining` counter.
- **Varints**: accept any ≤10-byte encoding (non-minimal included), drop bits past the 64th, raise on an eleventh byte; 32-bit readers take the low 32 bits.
- **Groups**: skipped with an explicit stack (no recursion-depth blowup), with end-tag field-number matching.
- **Lengths**: rejected above `2^31 - 1` *before* allocation, and payloads read in bounded chunks so hostile lengths fail cheaply.
- **Strings**: strict `@utf8.decode(..., ignore_bom=false)`.
- **Floats**: raw bit reinterpretation, bit-exact.

- `None` vs `Some("")` preserved; `host` is `Some(_)` exactly when an authority exists, holding bracketed literals (`"[::1]"`).
- `to_string` emits each delimiter exactly when its component is present, so `parse(uri.to_string()) == uri` (round-trip property).
- `resolve` transcribes Section 5.2 in strict mode (`http:g` → `http:g`), including the literal two-buffer `remove_dot_segments`, validated against all 23 normal and 19 abnormal §5.4 examples.
- Rejects forbidden raw characters, malformed percent-encoding, non-numeric ports, malformed IPv6/IPvFuture, ambiguous authorities, and invalid schemes.
